cd "/private/var/folders/kp/vdv61pd97vd0x29b257r8h7h0000gn/T/barcode-v8l_rnnm" && python3 -c "
from PIL import Image
im = Image.open('barcode.png').convert('RGB')
w,h = im.size
print(w,h)
# sample vertical center column colors for each x
import collections
cols=[]
for x in range(w):
    # average over middle rows to be robust
    rs=gs=bs=0
    n=0
    for y in range(h//4, 3*h//4):
        r,g,b = im.getpixel((x,y))
        rs+=r; gs+=g; bs+=b; n+=1
    cols.append((rs//n, gs//n, bs//n))
# find runs of similar color
runs=[]
start=0
def dist(a,b): return abs(a[0]-b[0])+abs(a[1]-b[1])+abs(a[2]-b[2])
for x in range(1,w):
    if dist(cols[x], cols[start])>30:
        runs.append((start,x-1,cols[start]))
        start=x
    else:
        # update running average color
        pass
runs.append((start,w-1,cols[start]))
for s,e,c in runs:
    print(f'x {s:4d}-{e:4d} width {e-s+1:4d} color {c}')
"

The image is a 1000×200 "video barcode" — each column is the average color of a moment in the video. I extracted the stripe sequence:

1. Creamy white (~6% at start) → hot pink (thin) → several light blues → **brown** → bright blue → **amber/gold** → pink → purple → rose → **big lime green** → lavender → blue → **rust/dark orange** → taupe → **long gray/olive/khaki ending (~22% of the video)**

***Masha and the Bear*** ([Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_language "Russian language"): Maша и Медвeдь, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Russian "Romanization of Russian"): *Masha i Medved'*, pronounced [\[ˈmaʂə ɪ mʲɪdˈvʲetʲ\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Russian "Help:IPA/Russian")) is a Russian [preschool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preschool "Preschool") [comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_comedy "Television comedy") animated television series created by Oleg Kuzovkov and produced by [Animaccord Animation Studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animaccord_Animation_Studio "Animaccord Animation Studio"), loosely based on the oral children's [folk story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folklore "Folklore") of the same name. The series focuses on the adventures of a very young girl named Masha and a bear (whom she dubs "Mishka"), her caring friend who always keeps her safe from disasters.

The episode "Recipe for Disaster" (Russian: Маша плюс каша, romanized: *Masha plyus kasha*) has over 4\.6 billion views on YouTube as of June 2026, making it the site's [sixteenth most viewed video of all time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most-viewed_YouTube_videos "List of most-viewed YouTube videos").[\[1\]](#cite_note-1)

The show was first launched on 7 January 2009\.[\[2\]](#cite_note-imdb-mashaandthebear-2)

The show provides the basis for the Masha and The Bear Land of Laughter, an area with attractions aimed at younger children at the theme park [The Land of Legends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Land_of_Legends "The Land of Legends"), near [Antalya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antalya "Antalya"), [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey").[\[3\]](#cite_note-3)

## Plot

Masha is a four-year-old girl who lives in the forest in an unspecified location in Russia (possibly in [Tver Oblast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tver_Oblast "Tver Oblast")) with her pig, goat, and dog. In the first episode, it is shown that all the animals in the forest are afraid of her, as she is constantly forcing them to play with her. Then Masha sees a butterfly and inadvertently follows it inside the home of the Bear, who has gone fishing. While playing there, she makes a big mess. When he returns, he sees the disaster caused by Masha. The Bear tries to get rid of Masha but after multiple failed attempts, the unlikely duo become friends.[\[4\]](#cite_note-4)

In each episode of the show, Masha is portrayed as a bright little girl who loves exploring the world around her. Masha's shenanigans result in unexpected but entertaining situations that are at the heart of the show's episodes. The kind-hearted Bear is always trying to keep Masha out of trouble. There are several supporting characters in the series, including Masha's cousin Dasha, a penguin adopted by the Bear, a young panda cub from China (the Bear's cousin), two wolves who live in an old [UAZ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UAZ-452 "UAZ-452") ambulance, a tiger that used to work with the Bear in the circus, and a Female Bear that is the object of the Bear's affections. Characters also include a hare, squirrels and hedgehogs, a pig called Rosie, a goat, and a dog who all live in Masha's front yard.[\[5\]](#cite_note-5)

## Characters

### Main characters

#### Masha

Masha is a 4-year-old girl who is portrayed as naughty and hyperactive, and always thinks about playing. She lives in a house near a [railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railway_station "Railway station"); near her house there is a path that leads to the Bear's house. Masha loves the bear very much, but in her games she tends to create problems for him. She loves sweets, jumping in a bucket, and looking at drawings of her and Bear. Masha's character combines the characteristics of 4-year-old (making grammatical errors when speaking, crying when she is not given what she wants, throwing tantrums) with adult skills (playing tennis, fishing, making preserves, playing electric guitar and speaking perfectly). In the episode "God Save the Queen", it is revealed that Masha has [super strength](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_strength "Super strength"), as she managed to pull a multi-ton train near her house just to give an elephant reception for the Lion King. She is voiced by Alina Kukushkina in Russian, and in English by [Elsie Fisher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elsie_Fisher "Elsie Fisher").[\[6\]](#cite_note-Reprints-6) In subsequent seasons, Masha was dubbed by Rebecca Bloom (ep. 28–39), Angelica Keamy (ep. 40–52), Kaitlyn McCormick (53–78, Masha’s Songs S4 EP 1), Adriana Figuredo (79-84) and now dubbed by West Rubin and Sofia Calasso. She is usually shown wearing a white shirt under a reddish-magenta dress with a reddish-magenta kerchief covering her short blonde hair.

#### Bear

The bear is a retired circus [brown bear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_bear "Brown bear") in [Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow "Moscow") who lives in a house hollowed out of a tree in the forest. His past occupation makes him very talented in performing arts (like juggling, unicycling, and even stage magic) although he's also known to dabble into other hobbies and even some intellectual pursuits. Some episodes feature flashbacks in which he remembers his childhood as a cub in the same house. In the Russian-language version, Masha calls him "Mishka" ([Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_language "Russian language"): Мишка, or named Medved in the intro), a diminutive form of the name [Mikhail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikhail "Mikhail") (i.e. "[Mikey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikey "Mikey")"), which is also the traditional name given to bears in [Russian tales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_fairy_tale "Russian fairy tale"). He is a huge bear with a big heart and he is Masha's father-like figure, as well as a friendly figure to her. He was voiced by Boris Kutnevich, Denis Naskarov and Irina Kukushkina. He became as pink as he is (a [Barbie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbie "Barbie")\-styled Bear) with his hair flipped at the end of "Shower Power".

#### Masha's pets

A [terrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrier "Terrier") (dog), a [goat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goat "Goat") and a [pig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pig "Pig") (and in the episode "How They Met", three [chickens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicken "Chicken")) who live outside Masha's house in her front yard (currently live in a well), but almost every time Masha comes out, they hide themselves to avoid her. The Pig is often forced to play with Masha, who makes it dress up like a baby in a stroller. In the episode "Dance Fever" it is revealed that the pig's name is Rosie. In the episodes "Laundry Day", "Growing Potion", "New Kids on the Block" and other episodes, it is revealed that the pig (Rosie) is a baby.

#### The wild animals

The wild animals are a [rabbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabbit "Rabbit"), [red squirrels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_squirrel "Red squirrel"), [hedgehogs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hedgehog "Hedgehog") and two [wolves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolf "Wolf"). Masha and a certain Hare—in "One, two three! Light the Christmas Tree", Father Frost's list calls him 'Bunny' (he was also named Bunny in "Tracks of Unknown Animals" and "No Trespassing"), and in "Surprise! Surprise!" he delivers painted eggs—often play hockey together. Bunny is occasionally an antagonist of the Bear, due to stealing carrots from the Bear's garden. The two Wolves live in a derelict ambulance car on top of a hill, often looking for something to eat, and act as medics for any apparent injuries or illnesses, though they sometimes fear Masha (living in an ambulance cab and acting as medics is a pun on the idiomatic expression, "wolves are orderlies of the woods").

#### Lady Bear

The Lady Bear is a female [brown bear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_bear "Brown bear"). The Bear has a crush on her and sometimes goes out of his way to impress her. The first time she rebuffed him in favor of the Black Bear, only to later realize how self-absorbed the Rival Bear is. Another time, she turned her nose up at the Bear's [classical guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_guitar "Classical guitar") playing as she preferred more modern music.[\[7\]](#cite_note-7) Even so, the She-Bear usually opens up to the Bear, such as the time she agreed to have a dinner with him, and she is sometimes kind to Masha, such as giving her a fashion magazine, helping to train her for her tennis match against the Black Bear, and helping her learn to ice-skate.

#### Dasha

Dasha is Masha's cousin from [Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow "Moscow"), who looks exactly like Masha, but is more "ladylike", has platinum-blonde hair and blue eyes (Masha's are green), wears boxy, blue-rimmed glasses and a red-orange dress. She is afraid of the Bear and calls him "Shaggy", "Monster" and "Beast".[\[8\]](#cite_note-8) She is voiced by [Alina Kukushkina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alina_Kukushkina "Alina Kukushkina").

#### Panda

Panda is a [panda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panda "Panda") cub and the Bear's young cousin from [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"). He and Masha are rivals, often bickering every time he comes for a visit, but they occasionally get along and have fun together.

### Recurring characters

#### King Lion III

A [lion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lion "Lion") wearing a [crown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown "Crown"), who is a good friend of the bear. He sometimes visits the bear, to play together the game of [chess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess "Chess") or for collective outdoor adventures. He was always disturbed by Masha, sometimes being advised to him not to help bear as a king is not supposed to help anyone. Once the lion offered his crown to Masha, making her a queen for temporary basis.

#### Whiskers n' Stripes

A [Siberian tiger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siberian_tiger "Siberian tiger") who is Bear's best friend from their days performing together in the [Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow "Moscow") circus.

#### Rival Bear

A [Himalayan black bear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himalayan_black_bear "Himalayan black bear"), who is Bear's worst enemy and Bear's chief rival for the attentions of the Lady Bear. The Rival Bear has an arrogant and unsportsmanlike personality, cheating to win against Masha in a tennis game, and laughing at her when she grows gigantic. Bear's biggest fear is if Black Bear and Lady Bear marry, which is shown in Game Over when Bear imagines what will happen if he plays games his whole life.

#### Penguin

An [Adélie penguin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adélie_penguin "Adélie penguin") that first appears in "The Foundling", as an egg that Masha finds and makes the Bear hatch. The Penguin quickly imprints on the Bear as his parental-figure and the Bear forms a sincere bond with him, but chooses to send the Penguin to live in Antarctica for his own health.[\[9\]](#cite_note-9) Even so, they stay in touch and the Penguin once visited.

#### Santa Claus (Father Frost)

[Santa Claus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Claus "Santa Claus") appears in Christmas-themed episodes.

#### Four-eyed aliens

A trio of alien specimens who accidentally crashed on [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth"). They were helped by Bear and Masha to get back to their spaceship.

#### January and Winter

They appeared in "The Legend of the Twelve Months". January only appeared in one Season 7 episode.

### Other Months

They also appeared in "The Legend of the Twelve Months". February and March only appeared in "Masha and the Bear Shorties" (April will appear in the 8th season of Masha and the Bear).

#### Tourists

They appear in "Princess and the Beast" (as usual appearances, they only did one).

#### Bear Impostor and His Assistant

They only appear in two episodes from Season 7\.

## Sources

According to the project's director, Denis Chervyatsov,

> Masha was based on a real person ... In the 1990s, the project's artistic director, Oleg Kuzovkov, was on holiday when he saw a little girl on the beach. The child was so genuine and open that she could easily walk up to a stranger and play chess with him or pick up his flippers and go swimming. However, after a few days, the vacationers began to hide from the girl – she was too active and intrusive.

[\[10\]](#cite_note-ustinova16-10)

The series' production has been handled domestically at Animaccord Animation Studio since 2008\.[\[10\]](#cite_note-ustinova16-10) The scenario for each episode is written by Oleg Kuzovkov, creator of the cartoon. Then the storyboarding is developed in accordance with the script and, in general, consists of at least 2000 slides. After the team finalizes the plot of an episode, the work for the 2D animatic kicks off. At this stage, animators define the duration of each scene in an episode, how characters are placed in it and interact with each other. After this step of the production is finished, the episode is passed for dubbing. Dubbing must be completed before 3D animation is applied, as the 3D animators need to know the characters' dialogue, intonations, and emotions in advance in order to keep their lip movements synchronized to the audio and make their facial expressions look realistic.[\[11\]](#cite_note-11)

## Actors

Masha, her cousin Dasha, and Father Frost are the only characters who speak. The others communicate through gibberish or wordless sounds.

For the first two seasons, Masha's voice in the original Russian version was performed by Alina Kukushkina, who was 6 years old when she began to dub Masha. For the third season (seven years later in 2015), the officials of Animaccord animation studio confirmed that the new voice of Masha would be 6-year-old Barbara Sarantseva and then replaced again by Yulia Zunikova in 2020\. The show's sound designer, Boris Kutnevich and Denis Naskarov, provide voices of Bear. Mark Kutnevich provides the voice of Bunny.

For the English version, [Elsie Fisher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elsie_Fisher "Elsie Fisher") – the voice of Agnes Gru in the *Despicable Me* films – dubbed the voice of Masha in the first season. In subsequent seasons Masha was dubbed by Rebecca Bloom (ep. 27-39) and Angelica Keamy (ep. 40–52), Kaitlyn McCormick (ep. 53-78), Adriana Figuredo (ep. 78-84) and now dubbed by West Rubin and Sofia Calasso.

## Soundtrack

The soundtrack for each episode is written by Russian composer Vasily Bogatyrev.\[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*\] Many compositions are stylized for famous works: [Moonlight Sonata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moonlight_Sonata "Moonlight Sonata"), [Beethoven's Symphony No. 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._5_\(Beethoven\) "Symphony No. 5 (Beethoven)"), a circus theme from the film *[Circus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circus_\(1936_film\) "Circus (1936 film)")*, and in the episode "One-Hit Wonder" the rockstar Masha performs a song in the style of the group [AC/DC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AC/DC "AC/DC"). Most of the songs used in the cartoon, such as the soundtracks of "Laundry Day" and "The Grand Piano Lesson" episodes, became popular in Russia and abroad.\[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*\]

## Reception

Within Russia, the influence of *Masha and the Bear* was the subject of debate. Detractors compared it negatively to Western children's shows and saw Masha's behaviour as setting a bad example for Russian children.[\[12\]](#cite_note-KommersantReview2016-12)[\[13\]](#cite_note-13) [Lidia Matveeva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lidia_Matveeva?action=edit&redlink=1 "Lidia Matveeva (page does not exist)") \[[ru](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Матвеева,%20Лидия%20Владимировна "ru:Матвеева, Лидия Владимировна")\], a professor at the Faculty of Psychology at [Moscow State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow_State_University "Moscow State University"), stated that Masha contradicts "traditional values" about the role of women and fathers in Russian society.[\[14\]](#cite_note-B17-14) She believes that Masha receives positive reinforcement for her disrespect towards the Bear, whom Matveeva described as both a [father figure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Father_figure "Father figure") and a [representation of Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Bear "Russian Bear"), and general disregard for social norms.[\[14\]](#cite_note-B17-14) Conversely, Egor Moskvitin of *[Ogonyok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ogonyok "Ogonyok")* argued that the show promotes progressive pedagogy, in that it portrays Masha learning from her mistakes through experience and gentle help from the Bear rather than through punishment.[\[12\]](#cite_note-KommersantReview2016-12)

The success of *Masha and the Bear* abroad was analysed both within and outside Russia. Moskvitin compared the slapstick style to that of [Leonid Gaidai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonid_Gaidai "Leonid Gaidai") and the [Marx Brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marx_Brothers "Marx Brothers"), which he believes appeals to a broad range of viewers across the world.[\[12\]](#cite_note-KommersantReview2016-12) Nataliya Vasilyeva of the [Associated Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Press "Associated Press") noted the show's popularity in many Muslim countries, particularly Indonesia, and attributed it to Masha's "folk costume with a headscarf".[\[15\]](#cite_note-BigStoryAP2016-15) A number of European politicians and media outlets have argued that *Masha and the Bear* is an instrument of Russian [soft power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_power "Soft power").[\[16\]](#cite_note-16)[\[17\]](#cite_note-17)[\[18\]](#cite_note-TheTimes2018-18)[\[19\]](#cite_note-Libération2017-19)[\[20\]](#cite_note-20)[\[21\]](#cite_note-21) [Priit Hõbemägi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priit_Hõbemägi?action=edit&redlink=1 "Priit Hõbemägi (page does not exist)") \[[et](https://et.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priit%20Hõbemägi "et:Priit Hõbemägi")\], an Estonian journalist and lecturer at [Tallinn University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tallinn_University "Tallinn University"), stated that the bear is a symbol commonly associated with Russia and that its portrayal in the show aims to form a positive image of the country in children.[\[22\]](#cite_note-22) [Mark Galeotti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Galeotti "Mark Galeotti"), a British historian and expert on Russia, argued that fears about *Masha and the Bear* were greatly exaggerated and risked fueling unnecessary censorship and xenophobic attitudes toward Russian culture.[\[23\]](#cite_note-23) Animaccord stated that their project is independent and they have never received funding from the Russian government.[\[15\]](#cite_note-BigStoryAP2016-15)[\[18\]](#cite_note-TheTimes2018-18) During the ongoing [Russo-Ukrainian war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russo-Ukrainian_war_\(2022–present\) "Russo-Ukrainian war (2022–present)"), the show is still accessible on YouTube in its Ukrainian-language version and remains highly popular in Ukraine.[\[24\]](#cite_note-24)

## Censorship

On 21 August 2026, Ukraine sanctioned Animaccord and other individuals involved in producing and distributing *Masha and the Bear* for allegedly spreading "pro-Russian narratives" and posing a threat to national security.[\[25\]](#cite_note-:0-25)[\[26\]](#cite_note-:1-26) The decision means that the show could no longer be broadcast in the country.[\[25\]](#cite_note-:0-25) A representative for Animaccord described the accusations as "false and defamatory" and noted that the studio operates independently and has never received funding from the Russian government.[\[25\]](#cite_note-:0-25)[\[26\]](#cite_note-:1-26)

Daddy Yankee with "[Despacito](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Despacito "Despacito")".\[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*\]

## Mobile apps

The first *Masha and the Bear* mobile app was released by Apps Ministry in August 2011\.\[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*\] In 2013 the first mobile game *Masha and the Bear: Search and Rescue* was published by Apps Ministry. Later more publishers such as Indigo Kids, PSV Studio, Noviy Disk developed and released games and apps featuring Masha and the Bear.\[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*\]

***Masha and the Bear*** ([Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_language "Russian language"): Maша и Медвeдь, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Russian "Romanization of Russian"): *Masha i Medved'*, pronounced [\[ˈmaʂə ɪ mʲɪdˈvʲetʲ\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Russian "Help:IPA/Russian")) is a Russian [preschool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preschool "Preschool") [comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_comedy "Television comedy") animated television series created by Oleg Kuzovkov and produced by [Animaccord Animation Studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animaccord_Animation_Studio "Animaccord Animation Studio"), loosely based on the oral children's [folk story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folklore "Folklore") of the same name. The series focuses on the adventures of a very young girl named Masha and a bear (whom she dubs "Mishka"), her caring friend who always keeps her safe from disasters.

The episode "Recipe for Disaster" (Russian: Маша плюс каша, romanized: *Masha plyus kasha*) has over 4\.6 billion views on YouTube as of June 2026, making it the site's [sixteenth most viewed video of all time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most-viewed_YouTube_videos "List of most-viewed YouTube videos").[\[1\]](#cite_note-1)

The show was first launched on 7 January 2009\.[\[2\]](#cite_note-imdb-mashaandthebear-2)

The show provides the basis for the Masha and The Bear Land of Laughter, an area with attractions aimed at younger children at the theme park [The Land of Legends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Land_of_Legends "The Land of Legends"), near [Antalya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antalya "Antalya"), [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey").[\[3\]](#cite_note-3)

## Plot

Masha is a four-year-old girl who lives in the forest in an unspecified location in Russia (possibly in [Tver Oblast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tver_Oblast "Tver Oblast")) with her pig, goat, and dog. In the first episode, it is shown that all the animals in the forest are afraid of her, as she is constantly forcing them to play with her. Then Masha sees a butterfly and inadvertently follows it inside the home of the Bear, who has gone fishing. While playing there, she makes a big mess. When he returns, he sees the disaster caused by Masha. The Bear tries to get rid of Masha but after multiple failed attempts, the unlikely duo become friends.[\[4\]](#cite_note-4)

In each episode of the show, Masha is portrayed as a bright little girl who loves exploring the world around her. Masha's shenanigans result in unexpected but entertaining situations that are at the heart of the show's episodes. The kind-hearted Bear is always trying to keep Masha out of trouble. There are several supporting characters in the series, including Masha's cousin Dasha, a penguin adopted by the Bear, a young panda cub from China (the Bear's cousin), two wolves who live in an old [UAZ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UAZ-452 "UAZ-452") ambulance, a tiger that used to work with the Bear in the circus, and a Female Bear that is the object of the Bear's affections. Characters also include a hare, squirrels and hedgehogs, a pig called Rosie, a goat, and a dog who all live in Masha's front yard.[\[5\]](#cite_note-5)

## Characters

### Main characters

#### Masha

Masha is a 4-year-old girl who is portrayed as naughty and hyperactive, and always thinks about playing. She lives in a house near a [railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railway_station "Railway station"); near her house there is a path that leads to the Bear's house. Masha loves the bear very much, but in her games she tends to create problems for him. She loves sweets, jumping in a bucket, and looking at drawings of her and Bear. Masha's character combines the characteristics of 4-year-old (making grammatical errors when speaking, crying when she is not given what she wants, throwing tantrums) with adult skills (playing tennis, fishing, making preserves, playing electric guitar and speaking perfectly). In the episode "God Save the Queen", it is revealed that Masha has [super strength](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_strength "Super strength"), as she managed to pull a multi-ton train near her house just to give an elephant reception for the Lion King. She is voiced by Alina Kukushkina in Russian, and in English by [Elsie Fisher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elsie_Fisher "Elsie Fisher").[\[6\]](#cite_note-Reprints-6) In subsequent seasons, Masha was dubbed by Rebecca Bloom (ep. 28–39), Angelica Keamy (ep. 40–52), Kaitlyn McCormick (53–78, Masha’s Songs S4 EP 1), Adriana Figuredo (79-84) and now dubbed by West Rubin and Sofia Calasso. She is usually shown wearing a white shirt under a reddish-magenta dress with a reddish-magenta kerchief covering her short blonde hair.

#### Bear

The bear is a retired circus [brown bear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_bear "Brown bear") in [Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow "Moscow") who lives in a house hollowed out of a tree in the forest. His past occupation makes him very talented in performing arts (like juggling, unicycling, and even stage magic) although he's also known to dabble into other hobbies and even some intellectual pursuits. Some episodes feature flashbacks in which he remembers his childhood as a cub in the same house. In the Russian-language version, Masha calls him "Mishka" ([Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_language "Russian language"): Мишка, or named Medved in the intro), a diminutive form of the name [Mikhail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikhail "Mikhail") (i.e. "[Mikey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikey "Mikey")"), which is also the traditional name given to bears in [Russian tales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_fairy_tale "Russian fairy tale"). He is a huge bear with a big heart and he is Masha's father-like figure, as well as a friendly figure to her. He was voiced by Boris Kutnevich, Denis Naskarov and Irina Kukushkina. He became as pink as he is (a [Barbie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbie "Barbie")\-styled Bear) with his hair flipped at the end of "Shower Power".

#### Masha's pets

A [terrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrier "Terrier") (dog), a [goat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goat "Goat") and a [pig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pig "Pig") (and in the episode "How They Met", three [chickens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicken "Chicken")) who live outside Masha's house in her front yard (currently live in a well), but almost every time Masha comes out, they hide themselves to avoid her. The Pig is often forced to play with Masha, who makes it dress up like a baby in a stroller. In the episode "Dance Fever" it is revealed that the pig's name is Rosie. In the episodes "Laundry Day", "Growing Potion", "New Kids on the Block" and other episodes, it is revealed that the pig (Rosie) is a baby.

#### The wild animals

The wild animals are a [rabbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabbit "Rabbit"), [red squirrels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_squirrel "Red squirrel"), [hedgehogs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hedgehog "Hedgehog") and two [wolves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolf "Wolf"). Masha and a certain Hare—in "One, two three! Light the Christmas Tree", Father Frost's list calls him 'Bunny' (he was also named Bunny in "Tracks of Unknown Animals" and "No Trespassing"), and in "Surprise! Surprise!" he delivers painted eggs—often play hockey together. Bunny is occasionally an antagonist of the Bear, due to stealing carrots from the Bear's garden. The two Wolves live in a derelict ambulance car on top of a hill, often looking for something to eat, and act as medics for any apparent injuries or illnesses, though they sometimes fear Masha (living in an ambulance cab and acting as medics is a pun on the idiomatic expression, "wolves are orderlies of the woods").

#### Lady Bear

The Lady Bear is a female [brown bear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_bear "Brown bear"). The Bear has a crush on her and sometimes goes out of his way to impress her. The first time she rebuffed him in favor of the Black Bear, only to later realize how self-absorbed the Rival Bear is. Another time, she turned her nose up at the Bear's [classical guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_guitar "Classical guitar") playing as she preferred more modern music.[\[7\]](#cite_note-7) Even so, the She-Bear usually opens up to the Bear, such as the time she agreed to have a dinner with him, and she is sometimes kind to Masha, such as giving her a fashion magazine, helping to train her for her tennis match against the Black Bear, and helping her learn to ice-skate.

#### Dasha

Dasha is Masha's cousin from [Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow "Moscow"), who looks exactly like Masha, but is more "ladylike", has platinum-blonde hair and blue eyes (Masha's are green), wears boxy, blue-rimmed glasses and a red-orange dress. She is afraid of the Bear and calls him "Shaggy", "Monster" and "Beast".[\[8\]](#cite_note-8) She is voiced by [Alina Kukushkina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alina_Kukushkina "Alina Kukushkina").

#### Panda

Panda is a [panda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panda "Panda") cub and the Bear's young cousin from [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"). He and Masha are rivals, often bickering every time he comes for a visit, but they occasionally get along and have fun together.

### Recurring characters

#### King Lion III

A [lion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lion "Lion") wearing a [crown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown "Crown"), who is a good friend of the bear. He sometimes visits the bear, to play together the game of [chess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess "Chess") or for collective outdoor adventures. He was always disturbed by Masha, sometimes being advised to him not to help bear as a king is not supposed to help anyone. Once the lion offered his crown to Masha, making her a queen for temporary basis.

#### Whiskers n' Stripes

A [Siberian tiger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siberian_tiger "Siberian tiger") who is Bear's best friend from their days performing together in the [Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow "Moscow") circus.

#### Rival Bear

A [Himalayan black bear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himalayan_black_bear "Himalayan black bear"), who is Bear's worst enemy and Bear's chief rival for the attentions of the Lady Bear. The Rival Bear has an arrogant and unsportsmanlike personality, cheating to win against Masha in a tennis game, and laughing at her when she grows gigantic. Bear's biggest fear is if Black Bear and Lady Bear marry, which is shown in Game Over when Bear imagines what will happen if he plays games his whole life.

#### Penguin

An [Adélie penguin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adélie_penguin "Adélie penguin") that first appears in "The Foundling", as an egg that Masha finds and makes the Bear hatch. The Penguin quickly imprints on the Bear as his parental-figure and the Bear forms a sincere bond with him, but chooses to send the Penguin to live in Antarctica for his own health.[\[9\]](#cite_note-9) Even so, they stay in touch and the Penguin once visited.

#### Santa Claus (Father Frost)

[Santa Claus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Claus "Santa Claus") appears in Christmas-themed episodes.

#### Four-eyed aliens

A trio of alien specimens who accidentally crashed on [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth"). They were helped by Bear and Masha to get back to their spaceship.

#### January and Winter

They appeared in "The Legend of the Twelve Months". January only appeared in one Season 7 episode.

### Other Months

They also appeared in "The Legend of the Twelve Months". February and March only appeared in "Masha and the Bear Shorties" (April will appear in the 8th season of Masha and the Bear).

#### Tourists

They appear in "Princess and the Beast" (as usual appearances, they only did one).

#### Bear Impostor and His Assistant

They only appear in two episodes from Season 7\.

## Sources

According to the project's director, Denis Chervyatsov,

> Masha was based on a real person ... In the 1990s, the project's artistic director, Oleg Kuzovkov, was on holiday when he saw a little girl on the beach. The child was so genuine and open that she could easily walk up to a stranger and play chess with him or pick up his flippers and go swimming. However, after a few days, the vacationers began to hide from the girl – she was too active and intrusive.

[\[10\]](#cite_note-ustinova16-10)

## Production

Unsourced material may be challenged and [removed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Burden_of_evidence "Wikipedia:Verifiability"). *(June 2016)* *([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance_template_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))* |
| --- | --- |

The series' production has been handled domestically at Animaccord Animation Studio since 2008\.[\[10\]](#cite_note-ustinova16-10) The scenario for each episode is written by Oleg Kuzovkov, creator of the cartoon. Then the storyboarding is developed in accordance with the script and, in general, consists of at least 2000 slides. After the team finalizes the plot of an episode, the work for the 2D animatic kicks off. At this stage, animators define the duration of each scene in an episode, how characters are placed in it and interact with each other. After this step of the production is finished, the episode is passed for dubbing. Dubbing must be completed before 3D animation is applied, as the 3D animators need to know the characters' dialogue, intonations, and emotions in advance in order to keep their lip movements synchronized to the audio and make their facial expressions look realistic.[\[11\]](#cite_note-11)

## Actors

Masha, her cousin Dasha, and Father Frost are the only characters who speak. The others communicate through gibberish or wordless sounds.

For the first two seasons, Masha's voice in the original Russian version was performed by Alina Kukushkina, who was 6 years old when she began to dub Masha. For the third season (seven years later in 2015), the officials of Animaccord animation studio confirmed that the new voice of Masha would be 6-year-old Barbara Sarantseva and then replaced again by Yulia Zunikova in 2020\. The show's sound designer, Boris Kutnevich and Denis Naskarov, provide voices of Bear. Mark Kutnevich provides the voice of Bunny.

For the English version, [Elsie Fisher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elsie_Fisher "Elsie Fisher") – the voice of Agnes Gru in the *Despicable Me* films – dubbed the voice of Masha in the first season. In subsequent seasons Masha was dubbed by Rebecca Bloom (ep. 27-39) and Angelica Keamy (ep. 40–52), Kaitlyn McCormick (ep. 53-78), Adriana Figuredo (ep. 78-84) and now dubbed by West Rubin and Sofia Calasso.

## Soundtrack

The soundtrack for each episode is written by Russian composer Vasily Bogatyrev.\[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*\] Many compositions are stylized for famous works: [Moonlight Sonata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moonlight_Sonata "Moonlight Sonata"), [Beethoven's Symphony No. 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._5_\(Beethoven\) "Symphony No. 5 (Beethoven)"), a circus theme from the film *[Circus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circus_\(1936_film\) "Circus (1936 film)")*, and in the episode "One-Hit Wonder" the rockstar Masha performs a song in the style of the group [AC/DC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AC/DC "AC/DC"). Most of the songs used in the cartoon, such as the soundtracks of "Laundry Day" and "The Grand Piano Lesson" episodes, became popular in Russia and abroad.\[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*\]

## Reception

Within Russia, the influence of *Masha and the Bear* was the subject of debate. Detractors compared it negatively to Western children's shows and saw Masha's behaviour as setting a bad example for Russian children.[\[12\]](#cite_note-KommersantReview2016-12)[\[13\]](#cite_note-13) [Lidia Matveeva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lidia_Matveeva?action=edit&redlink=1 "Lidia Matveeva (page does not exist)") \[[ru](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Матвеева,%20Лидия%20Владимировна "ru:Матвеева, Лидия Владимировна")\], a professor at the Faculty of Psychology at [Moscow State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow_State_University "Moscow State University"), stated that Masha contradicts "traditional values" about the role of women and fathers in Russian society.[\[14\]](#cite_note-B17-14) She believes that Masha receives positive reinforcement for her disrespect towards the Bear, whom Matveeva described as both a [father figure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Father_figure "Father figure") and a [representation of Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Bear "Russian Bear"), and general disregard for social norms.[\[14\]](#cite_note-B17-14) Conversely, Egor Moskvitin of *[Ogonyok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ogonyok "Ogonyok")* argued that the show promotes progressive pedagogy, in that it portrays Masha learning from her mistakes through experience and gentle help from the Bear rather than through punishment.[\[12\]](#cite_note-KommersantReview2016-12)

The success of *Masha and the Bear* abroad was analysed both within and outside Russia. Moskvitin compared the slapstick style to that of [Leonid Gaidai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonid_Gaidai "Leonid Gaidai") and the [Marx Brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marx_Brothers "Marx Brothers"), which he believes appeals to a broad range of viewers across the world.[\[12\]](#cite_note-KommersantReview2016-12) Nataliya Vasilyeva of the [Associated Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Press "Associated Press") noted the show's popularity in many Muslim countries, particularly Indonesia, and attributed it to Masha's "folk costume with a headscarf".[\[15\]](#cite_note-BigStoryAP2016-15) A number of European politicians and media outlets have argued that *Masha and the Bear* is an instrument of Russian [soft power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_power "Soft power").[\[16\]](#cite_note-16)[\[17\]](#cite_note-17)[\[18\]](#cite_note-TheTimes2018-18)[\[19\]](#cite_note-Libération2017-19)[\[20\]](#cite_note-20)[\[21\]](#cite_note-21) [Priit Hõbemägi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priit_Hõbemägi?action=edit&redlink=1 "Priit Hõbemägi (page does not exist)") \[[et](https://et.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priit%20Hõbemägi "et:Priit Hõbemägi")\], an Estonian journalist and lecturer at [Tallinn University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tallinn_University "Tallinn University"), stated that the bear is a symbol commonly associated with Russia and that its portrayal in the show aims to form a positive image of the country in children.[\[22\]](#cite_note-22) [Mark Galeotti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Galeotti "Mark Galeotti"), a British historian and expert on Russia, argued that fears about *Masha and the Bear* were greatly exaggerated and risked fueling unnecessary censorship and xenophobic attitudes toward Russian culture.[\[23\]](#cite_note-23) Animaccord stated that their project is independent and they have never received funding from the Russian government.[\[15\]](#cite_note-BigStoryAP2016-15)[\[18\]](#cite_note-TheTimes2018-18) During the ongoing [Russo-Ukrainian war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russo-Ukrainian_war_\(2022–present\) "Russo-Ukrainian war (2022–present)"), the show is still accessible on YouTube in its Ukrainian-language version and remains highly popular in Ukraine.[\[24\]](#cite_note-24)

## Censorship

On 21 August 2026, Ukraine sanctioned Animaccord and other individuals involved in producing and distributing *Masha and the Bear* for allegedly spreading "pro-Russian narratives" and posing a threat to national security.[\[25\]](#cite_note-:0-25)[\[26\]](#cite_note-:1-26) The decision means that the show could no longer be broadcast in the country.[\[25\]](#cite_note-:0-25) A representative for Animaccord described the accusations as "false and defamatory" and noted that the studio operates independently and has never received funding from the Russian government.[\[25\]](#cite_note-:0-25)[\[26\]](#cite_note-:1-26)

import json
import numpy as np
from PIL import Image

data=json.load(open('frame_colors.json'))
im=Image.open('barcode.png').convert('RGB')
w,h=im.size
arr=np.asarray(im,dtype=np.float32)
target=arr.mean(axis=0)  # (1000,3) column-average colors
N=1000

results={}
preds={}
for k,v in data.items():
    times=np.array(v['times']); colors=np.array(v['colors'])  # (n,3)
    length=v['length']
    # predicted color at each column: time fraction
    fr=(np.arange(N)+0.5)/N*length
    idx=np.abs(fr[:,None]-times[None,:]).argmin(axis=1)
    pred=colors[idx]
    preds[k]=pred
    d=np.abs(pred-target).sum(axis=1)
    results[k]=d.mean()
    # also chunked score (avg over 40 chunks) for robustness
    chunk=target.reshape(40,25,3).mean(axis=1), pred.reshape(40,25,3).mean(axis=1)
    c1,c2=chunk
    results[k+'_chunk40']=np.abs(c1-c2).sum(axis=1).mean()

for k in sorted(results, key=lambda x: results[x]):
    kk=k.replace('_chunk40','')
    print(f"{results[k]:8.2f}  {k:20s} ({data[kk]['length']}s, {data[kk]['n']} frames)")

# render predicted strips + target for visual check
rows_img=[]
def strip(a):
    return a[None,:,:].astype(np.uint8)  # 1x1000x3
target_u8=strip(target)
out=[target_u8]+[strip(preds[k]) for k in ['C_masha','H_babyshark','A_wheels','I_bath','F_phonics','B_miroshka','G_veggies','E_johny','D_baabaa','J_calvin']]
img=np.concatenate(out,axis=0)
Image.fromarray(img).resize((1000, img.shape[0]*40), Image.NEAREST).save('compare.png')
print('saved compare.png  rows: TARGET, masha, babyshark, wheels, bath, phonics, miroshka, veggies, johny, baabaa, calvin')
EOF

part.text:
Confirmed — and the frame montage explains every single stripe of the barcode:

- **0–6s**: white YouTube-search/Pinkfong intro → the **creamy white start**
- **6–8s**: hot-pink **Pinkfong logo screen** → the thin **hot pink stripe**
- **10–16s**: light-blue underwater baby shark → the **light blue blocks**
- **20–26s**: reddish-**brown coral wall** scene → the **brown block**
- **28–34s**: bright blue water (blue sharks) → **bright blue**
- **36–44s**: golden/yellow wall → **gold/amber**
- **46–52s / 54–60s / 62–68s**: pink (Mommy Shark) → purple (Grandma Shark) → crimson (Grandma/Grandpa) → the **pink → purple → rose sequence**
- **70–78s**: lime-green wall → the **big lime block**
- **80–82s**: lavender → **lavender**; 84–86s blue family shot → **thin blue**
- **88–94s**: rust-orange/brown cave scene → **rust orange blocks**
- **98–104s**: taupe "Safe at last" underwater rocks → **taupe**
- **108–116s**: pink "SUBSCRIBE" outro screens (pink+blue averages to gray-lavender) → **gray-lavender**
- **118–138s**: end-screen collage of video thumbnails (averages to khaki/olive) → the **long khaki-gray ending**

**Why this is conclusive:** I downloaded only YouTube hover-preview storyboard frames (no video streams) for all 10 candidates, computed each preview frame's average color, and reconstructed each video's barcode. Baby Shark Dance tracks the target within a few RGB points on essentially every stripe — mean per-pixel distance ≈ **30**, vs **130–245** for all nine other candidates (CoComelon entries, Johny Johny, Phonics Song, Miroshka eggs, and the dark Calvin Harris video). Four tiny deviations all land on scene transitions, an artifact of the 2-second preview spacing. The muted "gray ending" I initially found suspicious is actually Baby Shark's subscribe outro + thumbnail collage — which no other candidate shares.
